_about: Master content for the white-label Weekly Scam Alert. Tokens like {{CU_SHORT}} are filled per credit union by build.py from a brand file. Each issue is rewritten for a credit union audience from Scam Decoded research (source_issue = the Scam Decoded newsletter issue it draws on). No affiliate links, no product mentions, no Scam Decoded links in any member-facing text. [text](url) and **bold** are the only formatting.

issues.source: Scam Decoded newsletter #22 (breach follow-ups) and the fraud-call research behind it
issues.topic: Fake fraud department calls that ask for a code
issues.subject: Scam alert: if "we" call asking for a code, hang up
issues.preheader: Scammers pretend to be our fraud team. One rule stops them.
issues.headline: The fake fraud department call
issues.example: "Hi, this is the fraud department at {{CU_SHORT}}. We just stopped a $482 charge at an electronics store. To block it, I'm sending a code to your phone. Can you read it back to me?"
explain: The caller ID may even show our name. Caller ID is easy to fake.

That code isn't for blocking anything. It's the code that lets someone sign in to your account or approve a payment. Once you read it out, they can get in. Another version asks you to move your money to a "safe account" to protect it. There is no such thing.
issues.tell: Anyone who asks you to read back a code, give your password or PIN, or move money to keep it safe is not us.
steps: **Hang up.** Then call us at {{CU_PHONE}} or the number on the back of your card. If it was really us, we'll still be there.
**Already shared a code or moved money?** Call us right away at {{CU_PHONE}}. The sooner we know, the more we can try to do.
**Report it** at [ReportFraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov). It helps track who's behind these calls.
quick_hits: **A text first, then a call:** a text asks "Did you make this purchase? Reply YES or NO", then a "fraud agent" calls. Don't trust the call because of the text. Hang up and call us.
**"Don't tell the branch":** if a caller tells you to keep it secret from our staff, that's a scam every time.
issues.job: Save {{CU_PHONE}} in your phone as "{{CU_SHORT}} (real number)", and tell one family member the rule: we never ask you to read back a code.

lobby.headline: We will never ask you to read back a code.
bullets: Hang up. Call the number on your card.

social.caption: Scam alert: someone calls from "the {{CU_SHORT}} fraud department" and asks you to read back a code we just texted you. Hang up. That code lets them into your account. We will never ask you to read back a code, give your PIN or move money to a "safe account". If you're not sure, call us at {{CU_PHONE}} or the number on the back of your card.
social.alt: Scam alert from {{CU_SHORT}}: we will never ask you to read back a code. Caller ID can be faked. Hang up and call the number on your card. There is no real safe account.

brief.Members may ask: "Did you just call me about a charge?"
brief.What to say: "We never ask members to read back a code or move money to a safe account. Let's look at your account together right now."
brief.Escalate: If they shared a code or moved money: follow our fraud procedure today, check recent sign-ins and payees, and help them change their password.

issues.topic: Task job scams and the fake check that comes with them
issues.subject: Scam alert: the job that pays you, then asks you to pay
issues.preheader: January job scams, the check that bounces, and when to call us first.
issues.headline: The job that asks you to pay
issues.example: "Hi! I'm a recruiter with a digital marketing agency. Flexible remote work, 60 to 90 minutes a day rating products, $300 to $800 a day. Interested? Message me on WhatsApp."
explain: The first small payouts are real, to build trust. Then your "account" goes negative and you have to deposit money, often in crypto, to unlock your earnings. That money doesn't come back.
Another version mails you a check to buy equipment from their "vendor". The money can show up in your account before the check clears. When it bounces days later, you owe back what you spent or sent.
issues.tell: A real job never asks you to pay, deposit or buy anything to get paid, and never sends you a check to pass money on to someone else.
steps: **Don't reply.** Look the company up yourself and apply through its real careers page.
**Got a check from a new employer, buyer or stranger?** Call us at {{CU_PHONE}} before you spend or send any of it. We'd much rather answer a question than help clean up a bounced check.
**Already paid?** Stop, even if they say one more deposit releases your money. Report it at [ReportFraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov).
quick_hits: **Interviews by text only:** real employers meet you by video or in person.
**"Receive money and forward it":** a job that has you move money through your account is moving stolen money, and you can be held responsible.
issues.job: Forward this to the person in your life who's job hunting right now.

lobby.headline: A real job never asks you to pay to get paid.
bullets: A check to send money on will bounce.
Ask us before you spend a check from a stranger.

social.caption: Job hunting this January? Watch for the "task job": big pay for liking videos or rating products, then a deposit to unlock your earnings. Or a check to buy equipment from their vendor, which bounces after you've sent the money. A real job never asks you to pay to get paid. Got a check from someone new? Call us at {{CU_PHONE}} before you spend it.
social.alt: Scam alert from {{CU_SHORT}}: a real job never asks you to pay to get paid. No deposits to unlock earnings. A check to send money on will bounce. Ask us before you spend a check from a stranger.

brief.Members may ask: "When will this check clear? My new job sent it for equipment."
brief.What to say: "Funds showing as available doesn't mean the check is good. Can you tell me about the job? A check you're asked to send part of somewhere else is a common scam."
brief.Escalate: Follow our deposit hold and fraud procedures. If the member already sent money, note who it went to and how.

issues.source: Scam Decoded newsletter #9 (wrong-number texts that turn into crypto investing)
issues.topic: Wrong-number texts that turn into crypto "investments"
issues.subject: Scam alert: the wrong number that wants to be friends
issues.preheader: How a polite text turns into a crypto investment, and the rule that ends it.
issues.headline: The wrong number that becomes an investment
issues.example: "Hi Emma, are we still on for dinner Saturday? ... Oh sorry, wrong number! You seem nice though. Where are you based?"
explain: This one is patient. Weeks of friendly chat later, your new friend mentions how well they're doing on a crypto trading site and offers to show you how.
The site shows your balance growing. When you try to take money out, there's a "tax" or "fee" to pay first. The balance was never real, and the fees keep coming.
issues.tell: Anyone you've only met online who brings up investing, on a site or app they picked, is running a scam. A fee to withdraw your own money means there's no money.
steps: **Don't invest** through a link or app sent by someone you met online. Delete and block wrong-number texts instead of replying.
**About to buy crypto or send a wire for an investment?** Call us at {{CU_PHONE}} first, or stop by a branch. Talking it through with someone you trust is the best protection there is.
**Already invested?** Stop paying fees. Report it to the FBI at [IC3.gov](https://www.ic3.gov) and the FTC at [ReportFraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov).
quick_hits: **"Recovery" services** that promise to get your crypto back for a fee are often the same scammers coming back for more.
**Check before you invest:** you can look up an adviser or firm for free at [Investor.gov](https://www.investor.gov).
issues.job: Don't reply to any wrong-number texts this week. Delete and block. It's the cheapest scam protection there is.

lobby.headline: Met online? Don't invest with them.
bullets: A fee to withdraw means there's no money.
Talk to us before you buy crypto or wire money.

social.caption: It starts with "Sorry, wrong number!" and a friendly chat that lasts weeks. Then your new friend shows you a crypto site where your money seems to grow, until you try to withdraw and there's a fee. Don't invest with anyone you've only met online. About to buy crypto or send a wire for an investment? Talk to us first at {{CU_PHONE}}.
social.alt: Scam alert from {{CU_SHORT}}: met online? Don't invest with them. Don't reply to wrong-number texts. A fee to withdraw means there's no money. Talk to us before you buy crypto or wire money.

brief.Members may ask: "I need to send a wire to my trading account. It's urgent, there's a fee to release my profits."
brief.What to say: "Can I ask how you found this platform? Fees to release profits are a common sign of an investment scam. Let's take a minute before we send anything."
brief.Escalate: Follow our elder and vulnerable adult procedures where they apply, and our wire and crypto-purchase fraud checks.

issues.source: Scam Decoded newsletter #11 and #13 (IRS season texts, refund send-backs)
issues.topic: Fake IRS texts and refund scams at the start of tax season
issues.subject: Scam alert: the IRS isn't texting you
issues.preheader: Tax season fakes are out. One rule beats all of them.
issues.headline: The IRS isn't texting you
issues.example: "IRS: Your online account has been suspended. Verify your identity within 24 hours to release your refund: [link]"
explain: The link opens a copy of a real sign-in page. It takes your login, then asks for a photo of your driver's license "to confirm it's you". With both, someone can file a tax return in your name or get into your real account.
issues.tell: The IRS doesn't text or email you out of the blue about your refund or your account. Any message like this is fake, however official it looks.
steps: **Don't tap the link.** To check your real account, type **IRS.gov** into your browser yourself.

**Already entered your details?** Change that password now and follow the steps at the IRS's [Identity Theft Central](https://www.irs.gov/identity-theft-central). If you shared card or account numbers, call us at {{CU_PHONE}}.
**Report it.** Forward the text to **7726** (SPAM), then report it to the IRS using [these steps](https://www.irs.gov/help/report-fraud/report-fake-irs-treasury-or-tax-related-emails-and-messages).
quick_hits: **"We sent your refund by mistake":** if a refund you didn't expect lands in your account and someone asks you to send it back to them, don't. Call us first.
**The arrest call:** the real IRS doesn't threaten arrest or demand gift cards or crypto. Hang up.
issues.job: Get a free IRS Identity Protection PIN. It stops anyone else filing a return with your Social Security number. Start at [IRS.gov's Identity Theft Central](https://www.irs.gov/identity-theft-central) and make sure the address is irs.gov.

lobby.headline: The IRS isn't texting you.
bullets: Don't tap tax links in texts.
Unexpected refund and a send-it-back call? Ask us first.

social.caption: Tax season scam alert: a text says your IRS account is suspended and you must verify your identity to get your refund. It's fake. The IRS doesn't text you out of the blue about refunds. Don't tap. Type IRS.gov yourself. And if an unexpected refund lands in your account with a call asking you to send it back, call us first at {{CU_PHONE}}.
social.alt: Tax season scam alert from {{CU_SHORT}}: the IRS isn't texting you. Don't tap tax links in texts. Type IRS.gov yourself. Unexpected refund and a send-it-back call? Ask us first.

brief.Members may ask: "The IRS deposited a refund by mistake and says I have to send it back by gift card or wire."
brief.What to say: "The IRS won't ask you to send a refund back that way. Let's not send anything yet and look at where this deposit came from."
brief.Escalate: Check the deposit source, follow our fraud and account-takeover procedures, and point the member to IRS.gov for the real return process.
